title: The Sinner's Shop Guide
dek: Nineteen-forty-one to now: where Seattle gets inked, sorted by what you want on your skin.
body: Seattle has been getting tattooed since before the Space Needle. Here's where to go, sorted by style. Call ahead: most of these are appointment-first, and lineups change.
## Old school and history
= Seattle Tattoo Emporium · Capitol Hill | Since 1941

Founded by C.J. 'Danny' Danzl, on Boren Avenue since 1999, and counted among the oldest working tattoo shops in the country. Owners Romie and James de Hillary took over in 2017 and keep a history-of-tattooing exhibit on the walls. Walk-ins welcome.
> It's important to either document and keep these places alive and going. (Romie de Hillary)
= Madame Lazonga's · Pike Place area | Since 1979
The studio of Vyvyn Lazonga, Seattle's First Lady of Tattoo. More on her in this issue's Skin Deep.
## American traditional
= Anchor Tattoo · Ballard | Small traditional shop
= White Lotus · Lake City | Eastern and American traditional
= Hidden Hand · Fremont | Since 2007, flash and custom
= Supergenius · Capitol Hill | Big crew, walk-ins
Hidden Hand and Supergenius co-organized the Seattle Tattoo Expo, so these crews know everyone.
## Japanese
= Strictly Irezumi · Greenwood | Japanese irezumi, appointment only
## Black and gray, realism
= Black Sparrow · Capitol Hill | Black-and-gray photorealism
= Fenix Tattoo & Piercing · Pioneer Square | Since 2000, realism and traditional
= Side Quest · Capitol Hill | Realism and neo-traditional
## Fine line and delicate
= Finer Things · Westlake | Fine line specialist, opened 2022
= Nightshade · Queen Anne | Fine line, antique-traditional, no AI designs
= Korazon · Greenwood | Fine line, realism and hand-poke
## Queer-owned and community
= True Love Tattoo · Capitol Hill | LGBTQIA-centric, gallery shows
= Lilith Tattoo · Central District | Queer-owned, appointment only
## The long runners
= Slave to the Needle · Ballard & Wallingford | Ballard since 1995
= Laughing Buddha · Capitol Hill | Since 1996, tattoos and piercing
= Moonlight Tattoo · Roosevelt | A local favorite
Shops change hands and artists move. Check a shop's own site and Instagram before you book, and look at healed work, not just fresh photos.

title: Skin Deep: The First Lady of Seattle Ink
dek: Skin Deep is back. First up: Vyvyn Lazonga, who picked up a tattoo machine when no other woman in Seattle would.
body: Skin Deep was a Sinner institution, and it's back. We start with the woman who broke the door down.

Vyvyn Lazonga was born in Seattle in 1947. In the early 1970s she apprenticed under C.J. 'Danny' Danzl at Seattle Tattoo Emporium, at a time when no other women were tattooing in this city. In 1979 she opened her own shop, one of the first female-owned tattoo parlors in the country.

Her work landed in the cult book 'Modern Primitives.' She won Best Tattooed Female in 1978 and the artists' choice award at the 2005 National Tattoo Association convention. She still runs Madame Lazonga's near Pike Place Market, and she does mastectomy-scar cover-ups, turning surgery into art.
> I always felt strong and powerful about it, and I still do. (Vyvyn Lazonga, on her full sleeves)
She's not a fan of where some of the industry is headed. Asked about computer-generated tattoo art, she told Seattle magazine it's disrespectful to the craft.
## The new blood

Dani Silva of Side Quest on Capitol Hill has been tattooing about 15 years and calls her style realism. Her own first tattoo? A memorial for a friend's initials, 'literally in Microsoft Word font,' she told KUOW. Everybody starts somewhere.

Shannon Perry, tattooer and musician, told The Stranger at last year's Expo that she likes her tattoos a little mischievous. And Moonlight Tattoo owner Bryan Kachel had a warning for the youngest clients: most 18-year-olds don't know who they are yet.
Know a Seattle artist who belongs in Skin Deep? Hit the Submit page.

title: The Law of the Needle
dek: What Washington actually requires before anyone puts ink in your skin, and what a shop can get busted for.
body: Every tattoo artist, body piercer and body-art artist in Washington needs a state license from the Department of Licensing, under RCW 18.300. So does every place that does the work: a shop, a mobile unit, even a one-off event.
= Artist license, per year | $275
= Shop, mobile unit or event license, per location | $330
= Late renewal, artist / shop | $385 / $440

To get licensed, an artist has to be at least 18 and hold a current bloodborne pathogens certificate. Shops need insurance, zoning and fire-code compliance, and have to meet sanitation standards. The state says it inspects every shop on a two-year rotation and investigates written complaints.
## The under-18 rule

Tattooing anyone under 18 in Washington is a misdemeanor under RCW 26.28.085, even with a parent standing right there. 'I didn't know' isn't a defense unless the artist made a real effort, like checking photo ID. The law even counts procedures that leave a visible scar. A Seattle defense firm says the penalty runs up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine. Doctors are exempt.
Plenty of shops go further. Nightshade on Queen Anne says flat out: no minors, even with parental permission.
## Beyond ink

The state's medical commission says tongue splitting, flesh hooks and implants are the practice of medicine and should only be done by licensed medical professionals. Branding and scarification count as body art. More on that in Beyond Ink.
Bottom line: before you sit down, ask to see the license. A real shop will be proud to show it.

title: The Regret Economy
dek: A quarter of tattooed Americans regret at least one. Here's what it costs to make it go away.
body: Your ex's name. That Chinese character that turned out to mean 'soup.' According to Pew, 24 percent of tattooed Americans regret at least one of their tattoos. Somebody's making money on that.
## Who's getting lasered

A huge removal-clinic database presented at a dermatology meeting in 2025 covered 560,042 tattoos. Nearly 70 percent of the patients were 18 to 39. Almost half the tattoos were on highly visible spots like the forearm, hand or face, and three-quarters were black ink. Illustrative and blackwork styles each made up 26 percent of removals.
A Louisiana clinic owner reported this fall that the crowd is getting younger, mostly removing ink they got between 16 and 22.
## What it costs around here
= Kirkland clinic, per business-card-size area | $99 / session
= Bellevue clinic, small to large | $500–$1,000 / session
= Bellevue picosecond-laser clinic range | $100–$800 / session

Most tattoos take several sessions spaced six to eight weeks apart. One Bellevue clinic says newer picosecond lasers can get it done in four to eight sessions instead of 10 to 15. That's the clinic's own claim, so ask for before-and-afters. Insurance doesn't cover it.
> We're seeing a much younger crowd trying to get tattoo removal than we ever have before. (Abbie Woodard, Louisiana Laserderm)
The Sinner's advice is cheaper than any laser: sleep on it. Then sleep on it again.

sources.title: Tattoo popularity grows, so does demand for removal

title: Piercing Now
dek: Faux rooks, back dimples and the comeback of the tongue ring. Plus the one tool a real piercer will never touch.
body: If your ears look like a jewelry store, you're right on trend. Bustle's 2026 roundup calls it maximalist 'earscaping,' and the hot placements this year are the faux rook, the hidden helix, the tragus-and-conch combo, back-dimple dermals, the floating industrial, and some Y2K throwbacks: navel and tongue.
> Surprisingly, I've seen a surge in tongue piercings recently (Roze Rahim, Nine Moons Piercing)
## How long it takes to heal
= Tongue | about 4–6 weeks
= Floating industrial | about 9–12 months
= Tragus-and-conch combo | up to a year
Those are piercers' estimates. Cartilage is slow. Don't sleep on it, don't twist it, don't swap the jewelry early.
## The gun is dead

The Association of Professional Piercers says piercing guns are never appropriate. Even the mall-friendly chain Studs uses needles only; its co-founder says guns have plastic parts that can't be sterilized and that needles are much more precise. Jewelry should be implant-grade titanium or solid gold.

Seattle has plenty of pro piercers; Laughing Buddha and Fenix on our Shop Guide both pierce. Ask what they use, ask to see the needle come out of a sealed package, and walk if anyone reaches for a gun.

title: What's in the Ink?
dek: The FDA found bacteria in a third of sealed tattoo inks, even ones labeled sterile. Here's what that means, and what the cancer headlines don't.
body: You check that the needle comes out of a sealed pack. But what about the ink?

In August, an FDA-led analysis in Scientific Reports pooled four FDA investigations from 2018 to 2024 covering 259 unopened ink jars. About 35 percent were contaminated with bacteria, and 30.5 percent of the inks labeled sterile were contaminated too. Thirty-four of the 94 bacterial species found have been linked to human disease. The study didn't measure whether the inks actually caused infections.
> an ink can be contaminated even if the container is sealed. (FDA)
## Recalls

In 2024 the FDA announced a recall of three Bloodline pigments for high levels of microorganisms. In May 2025 it warned about two Sacred Tattoo Ink lots, Raven Black and Sunny Daze, contaminated with bacteria including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
## Who regulates this stuff

Tattoo ink counts as a cosmetic. Under a 2022 law, the FDA started enforcing facility registration, product listings and adverse-event reporting in July 2024, and issued final guidance on preventing contamination that October. Europe went further: since 2023, two popular pigments, Blue 15:3 and Green 7, have been restricted, and a 'save the pigments' petition drew more than 175,000 signatures.
## The cancer question

A Swedish study in 2024 estimated a 21 percent higher lymphoma risk among tattooed people. A Danish twin study in 2025 found links to skin cancer and lymphoma, stronger for tattoos bigger than your palm. Neither proves tattoos cause cancer, and outside experts called the early findings possibly overstated. The Swedish lead researcher put it plainly: lymphoma is rare, and the results apply at the group level.
Takeaway: ask your artist what brand they use and whether it's from a reputable maker. Watch for redness, swelling or pain that gets worse instead of better, and see a doctor if it does.

title: Ink at Work
dek: A third of Americans are tattooed. The law still says your boss can make you cover up.
body: Thirty-two percent of American adults have a tattoo, according to Pew, and 80 percent say society has gotten more accepting. But 29 percent of people without tattoos still say they have a negative impression of people who have them. Some of them do the hiring.
## What the law says

Short answer: tattoos aren't a protected class under federal law. An employer can make you cover up. The exception is religion. When a Red Robin server was fired for refusing to cover religious wrist tattoos, the EEOC got involved and the case settled for $150,000.
## What the research says

A Colorado State University study found women applicants with visible tattoos were less likely to be hired for a supervisor job and, when hired, were offered lower starting pay, about $2,159 less for even a mild tattoo.
> We were shocked at how hard it is to overcome discrimination based on tattoos. (Chris Henle, Colorado State University)

A Queen's University researcher found the type of tattoo matters: 'friendly' ink barely registered with coworkers, while intimidating designs drew more bias. And workers who cover up say it makes them feel they aren't being their authentic selves.

Seattle's service and tech crowds are about as ink-friendly as it gets, but no Washington law has your back. Know your dress code before your interview, and know that a religious tattoo is a different story legally.

title: Convention Season
dek: The Seattle Tattoo Expo was in August. Here's where the needles go next.
body: You missed the big one. The Seattle Tattoo Expo, billed by Seattle Center as the Northwest's largest tattoo event, ran August 14 to 16 at Seattle Center's Exhibition Hall. Last year's drew more than 250 artists. Watch for 2027 dates.
In the meantime, here's the road trip:
= Boise Tattoo Convention · Riverside Hotel, Boise | Oct 23–25, 2026
= Vancouver Tattoo & Arts Festival · Vancouver Convention Centre | Jan 8–10, 2027
= Tacoma Tattoo Expo · Tacoma Dome | Mar 12–14, 2027
= Evergreen Tattoo Invitational · Lane Events Center, Eugene | Mar 19–21, 2027
= VOID Tattoo Fest · Jupiter Hotels, Portland | May 21–23, 2027
= Kamloops Tattoo Show · McArthur Island, Kamloops | Jun 11–13, 2027

Tacoma's is the closest and in its second year. Portland's VOID is the weird one: artists tattoo in converted motel rooms and there's a free Saturday street fair. Vancouver runs an adults-only Friday night.
Pro tip: the best artists book convention slots weeks ahead. DM them now. Eugene and Kamloops dates come from a single listing site, so confirm before you book a room.

title: Beyond Ink
dek: Tongue splits, flesh hooks and implants. Where the law draws the line on body mod.
body: Ink is the gateway. Some people go further: split tongues, scarification, magnets under the skin, hanging from hooks.
## Washington's line

The state's Medical Quality Assurance Commission says tongue splitting, body hooks and subdermal or transdermal implants are the practice of medicine. Translation: only licensed medical professionals should do them. Branding and scarification are treated as body art under a 2009 law. The commission also applies the logic of the under-18 tattoo ban to extreme mods, since they're even more permanent.
## Other states

Illinois was the first to regulate tongue splitting in 2003, limiting it to licensed practitioners. New York only lets doctors and dentists do it; a first offense is a misdemeanor and a repeat can be a felony. Georgia bans flesh-hook suspension outright, and Nevada effectively bans it unless a medical professional does it.
## Hanging by the skin
Suspension has had a dedicated scene since the first convention in Dallas in 2001. Practitioners describe it as ritual, not stunt.
> And it stops hurting — that's the interesting part of suspension. (Beto Rea, suspension practitioner)
Seattle's Pan Eros Foundation once hosted a suspension workshop in Pioneer Square, but we haven't found recent public events here. If you know the scene, tell us through the Submit page.
If you're thinking about anything on this page, find out who's legally allowed to do it before you find out the hard way.

title: AI Flash
dek: Clients are walking in with AI-generated tattoo designs. Artists hate it, and the law says nobody owns them.
body: Your cousin asked a chatbot for 'a wolf howling at a galaxy, fine line.' Now he wants it on his ribs. Tattoo artists are seeing this every day.

In Australia, one Adelaide artist told ABC News about one in four enquiries now come with AI images; another studio said closer to three in four. Artists say the designs come with misspelled words and extra fingers, and the software has no idea how a tattoo heals or ages in skin.
> You're going to come up with a weird tattoo that you can't really read. (Stu Pagdin, tattoo artist)
## Who owns it

Probably nobody. The U.S. Copyright Office concluded in January 2025 that work generated entirely by AI can't be copyrighted, and that typing a prompt, even a detailed one, doesn't make you the author. Only the human parts of a mixed work can be protected.
Tattoo copyright fights do happen with human art. In 2024 a jury found Kat Von D's Miles Davis tattoo wasn't substantially similar to the photographer's portrait it was based on.
## Seattle's take

Vyvyn Lazonga, tattooing here since the '70s, calls computer-generated tattoo art disrespectful to the craft. Nightshade on Queen Anne advertises that every design is hand-drawn, no AI. Bring your ideas and your references. Let the artist draw it.

title: Dressed to Sin
dek: Where Seattle's freaks, punks and vintage queens still shop.
body: The mall can't dress you. These places can. Check hours before you go; small shops move and close.
= Pretty Parlor · Capitol Hill | Retro party dresses, fur capes, kitten heels
= Indian Summer · Capitol Hill | '60s dresses, '90s crop tops
= Red Light Vintage · U District | Every decade, plus costumes
= Bon Voyage Vintage · Pioneer Square | Grungy Seattle style, local designers
= Doll Parts Collective · West Seattle | All sizes and gender expressions
= Winner's Circle · Capitol Hill | Skate and street, back on Broadway
= Georgetown Trailer Park Mall · Georgetown | Weekend throwback market and oddities

Winner's Circle reopened last November at 233 Broadway E, in the space left when Revival closed after 11 years. Georgetown Trailer Park Mall is a weekend-only lot of vintage trailers selling throwback clothes, folk art and, in Seattle Met's words, bizarre ephemera.
## Mark your calendar

The Punk Rock Flea Market has run on Capitol Hill for nearly two decades, at the old QFC on 15th Ave E: about 200 vendors, a buck to get in, proceeds to the Low Income Housing Institute. The next one is set for December.
> an anti-capitalist shopping spree in the magic factory we call the Quality Flea Center (Punk Rock Flea Market organizers)
We know this list is light on real goth shops. If Seattle still has one, tell us through the Submit page and we'll run it.

title: Stick-and-Poke Nation
dek: A needle, some ink and a dorm room. What doctors want you to know before you DIY.
body: Stick-and-poke is about as punk as tattooing gets: no machine, just a needle and ink, one dot at a time. It blew up on social media during the 2020 lockdowns, and online kits sell it as a cheap alternative to a shop.
## The risks

A Cleveland Clinic infectious-disease doctor lists staph, MRSA, hepatitis, HIV, allergic reactions and stubborn mycobacterial infections as risks of home tattoo kits, and calls them potentially extremely dangerous. UW Health warns that any shared needle can carry hepatitis B or C or HIV, and that pen ink isn't made for skin. A Mount Sinai dermatologist put it bluntly: ballpoint ink is not manufactured to be injected into the human body.
> Even though you might think you're sterilising your equipment with alcohol, sometimes it's not enough (Jamie Kim, dermatology PA)
## The legit version

Hand-poke isn't the problem. The kitchen table is. Professional hand-poke uses the same sterile needles, real tattoo ink and the same depth control as machine work. In Seattle, Korazon Tattoo in Greenwood offers it.
And remember the law: in Washington, tattooing anyone under 18 is a misdemeanor, machine or not.
Love the look? Get it done by someone with a license and a sharps container.
